title: Chapter 68 – Outer Sect Disciple
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The bell rings at dawn, and eight boys fall out of their beds onto the same patch of mud.

It is a long, flat, brazen note, struck by a servant at the end of the lane with a wooden mallet. Ma Bao is up first, grinning, still half asleep, hauling on his gray robe back to front. The silent boy has a hand over his face. The sharp-faced one, whose name is Pei, swears with great fluency at a stolen apple core that has turned up in his shoe. Jian is on his feet before the second stroke. He has not slept.

The knot under his bed rail is still there. He has looked at it twice in the dark. He has not touched it.

"First morning," says Ma Bao, with the cheerful air of a man announcing the weather. He is thirteen, broad and fair, with a farmer's hands and a voice that carries. "You get up. You wash at the spring. You eat at the long hall, if you have the points. You go to the duty board. If you are late, it is a point off. If you are very late, it is two, and the Deacon looks at you."

"The Deacon?"

"Mo Lian. He keeps the book." Ma Bao tugs his belt tight. "He is a good sort. Round as a bun. He gave me a rice cake on the second day." He lowers his voice. "Pei says he gives rice cakes to everyone he means to ask a favor of."

"Pei says a great deal," says Pei, from the door.

They go down the lane in the gray light with their wooden bowls, past the low wall and the wet reeds, and Jian listens. It is a thing he is good at. By the time they reach the spring he has the shape of the place.

There are tiers. They are carved on a stone at the head of the lane, in characters worn smooth by a hundred years of thumbs: Servant. Outer. Inner. Core. True. Beyond them, in a smaller hand, a sixth: Personal. The servants wear brown and do the work of the mountain for bed and bread, and may sit the Mirror again when they have saved the fee. The Outer wear gray. They have a courtyard to share, an allowance of three stones and a pill, and a duty. The Inner wear blue, and sleep in courtyards with their own springs and thicker air. The Core have peaks. The True have an Elder's name behind them.

A Personal disciple is another matter. He is an Elder's own, taken into his house, taught his arts, and fed from his stores. A Personal disciple does not have a duty board. He has a master.

A master, thinks Jian. And a master has obligations, and so does what he takes in.

"How does one get from Outer to Inner?" he asks.

Ma Bao laughs, kindly, as at a child. "You pass the Assessment. Fifth month of every year, after the Register. Anyone at the ninth layer who has enough points." He shrugs. "Nobody has made it in the first year since the Sect was founded. It takes four, five, six. If you are lucky. Or if someone with a name wants you."

"Wants me?"

"For his house." Ma Bao shrugs again. "That is what the Elders do. They watch the Assessment, and they pick. You do not apply. You are chosen." A pause. "Or you are not."

They reach the spring. It is a trickle from a cleft in a rock, collected in a stone trough, and a line of boys stands waiting with bowls. Jian drinks. The water is cold and tastes of iron.

The points, he learns, are the whole of the world.

He sees it at the long hall at breakfast, where the servants ladle gray millet into bowls and a clerk at a side table marks a slate. A bowl costs one point. A bowl with a boiled egg costs two. A bowl with meat is a luxury, and the boys who have it eat with their backs to the wall. The slate is a copy of the Contribution Register, and the Register is kept in the Outer Affairs Hall by a Deacon and a dozen clerks. It records every boy's name, his earnings, and his debts.

"They give you thirty on credit," says Pei, spooning millet with the air of a man at a funeral. "First month. For food. You pay it back by duty. One point a day, if you do your terrace. Thirty days and you are even. Miss a day, you start again."

"And if you are sick?"

"Then you are sick and in debt." Pei shrugs. "That is how they keep you."

Jian looks at his bowl. It is clean. It is, in its way, the most honest thing he has been given in a week.

Debt, he thinks. Thirty points. And a Deacon with rust-colored ink who would like to forgive it.

* * *

The duty board is a wall of black slate beside the Outer Affairs Hall, and his name is on it already.

Lin Jian. 0417. Medicine Valley, Terrace Nine. Dawn to noon.

He walks there alone, up a long, winding path through terraced fields of pale green, with a hoe on his shoulder and the sun coming up gold behind the peaks. The Valley lies in the mountain's western fold, sheltered from the wind, a great sloping bowl of black soil cut into a hundred small steps. It is the Sect's garden. It is the Sect's pharmacy, its larder, its quiet engine. Every pill that leaves the Pill Hall begins in these beds.

He has not been in a garden like it. He has been in one that was better, and one that was older. But never one so tended.

Every bed has a plaque, set on a stone at its corner: a number, a name, a date of planting, a harvest, a warden's mark. Some are small, no bigger than a table. Some run the length of a field. A row of boys in gray moves along them with baskets and hoes, kneeling, weeding, turning the soil with their hands. Over all of it lies a faint pale shimmer, a net of Qi stretched over the whole slope, hung from posts of white stone at the terrace corners.

An array, he thinks. Over the whole Valley. A guard, and a growth-aid, and a count.

"Lin Jian?"

The voice is a woman's, low and dry. She stands at the top of the path with a ledger under one arm: tall, thin, perhaps fifty, in a gray robe with a green sash and a face like a closed gate. She looks him over without hurry.

"Terrace Nine. Frostbell, Mourner's Cup, and the east end of the marrow beds. Weed, water, count." She holds out a flat wooden tally. "Every stem has a number. If a number is missing at noon, you answer for it. If a stem is damaged, you answer for it. If a root is damaged, you answer for it to me." A pause, exactly measured. "I am Overseer Han. I have never lost a bed. I would prefer not to begin."

"Yes, Overseer."

She walks away without another word.

He works.

It is a good kind of work. He kneels in a bed of Frostbell, small and blue and bitter, each flower on its own thin stem, and counts them with his fingers as he weeds. One. Two. The soil is rich and dark and smells of rain. It is quiet. Beyond the bed, on the next terrace, a half-dozen older boys are laboring over a long plot of something dense and dark, a tangle of thick purple vines with leaves like hands. A plaque at the corner reads Ninefold Marrow Vine. Level 2. The stems are as thick as his wrist. They are strung on poles of white stone, wrapped in cords of red thread.

Ninefold marrow vine, he thinks.

It is the first of the five. It is the thing Mu's slips named, the one ingredient of the Nine Turn pill that Qinghe could not buy, at any price, in any market, in the whole of the Ford.

He does not look up. He does not slow his hands. He weeds the Frostbell and counts the stems, and from the edge of his eye he watches the older boys cut a single, thick, pale shoot from the vine, with a bone knife, and lay it on a tray, and carry it, under the eye of a guard, to a small stone hut at the end of the terrace.

A guard, he thinks. At the hut. Two. And a tally.

It is not here for me, he thinks. Not yet. It is here for someone with a name.

At the end of the second hour, a clerk comes down the terrace with a small bronze bell, and the boys rise and straighten and file toward a row of low sheds where the day's wages are counted. He is given a thin slip of bamboo. One point. He folds it and puts it in his sleeve.

Twenty-nine, he thinks. And I owe a Deacon something I have not been asked for.

* * *

His father is in the corridor of the Enforcement Hall, with two guards and a cup of water.

Jian has not expected it. He had been told by a clerk, in a bored voice, that the Patriarch of the Lin clan had arrived at the Gate at first light, and been taken to the Hall of Open Session, and that no one under the Inner rank was permitted within a hundred paces. He had gone anyway. He is a boy with a hoe, in a gray robe, and nobody has stopped him.

It is a long, bare, echoing passage of dark stone, lined with benches. Wenyuan sits on the last of them, alone, with his back very straight and his hands folded in his lap. The bandaged one is still bandaged. He has put on his best tunic, the dark blue one with the plain gray hem, and has combed his hair. He looks older than he did a month ago. He looks, Jian thinks, like a man who has spent a night composing a speech he will never be allowed to give.

The guards see the boy. They look at each other.

"A minute," says the elder of them, with a small, stiff shrug. "He is a witness. It is not allowed." He turns his back, with an exaggerated care. "I have not seen anything."

Jian crosses the floor.

He does not say anything. He stops in front of the bench, and his father looks up, and for a moment the two of them simply regard each other, in the cold gray light from the high window.

"You are in the Reed Courtyard," says Wenyuan.

"Yes."

"I asked the clerk. It is the lowest." He does not sound angry. He sounds like a man reading a ledger. "I will speak to the Outer Affairs Hall. I will say..."

"Please do not."

"Jian..."

"It is where I can see." He says it quietly. "It is where the knot was. I would rather know where it is than have it moved."

Wenyuan's face changes. It is a small, quick, terrible change, like a window closing.

"A knot," he says.

"A Blood Shadow thread. Under my bed." He sits on the bench beside his father and keeps his voice very low. "Someone has chosen where I sleep. It is not a coincidence. I do not know who. I am going to find out."

"You are ten."

"I know."

"I should take you home."

"You cannot." He does not make it a challenge. He says it as a fact, gently, as one might tell a man the sun will rise. "And I should not go. If I go, it follows. If I stay, I can watch it."

Wenyuan is quiet for a very long time.

Down the corridor, a door opens. A clerk in gray puts out his head and looks at them with a disapproving eye, and the elder guard clears his throat, loudly, and the head withdraws.

"Your mother wrote you a letter," says Wenyuan at last. He puts his good hand into his sleeve and takes out a small flat packet, tied with blue thread. "It has no numbers. Your sister wrote one line. You will find it at the bottom." He lays it on the boy's knee. "I did not read either."

"Thank you."

"I will be in the Hall until the evening. After that, I am told, I am to be lodged at the guest house until the end of the Register. I do not know whether I shall see you." He turns his head, very slightly. "I shall be watching the Elders. All nine. I have a list of their names."

"What will you do with it?"

"I do not know." The ghost of a dry smile crosses his face. "I am a talisman master. I draw lines. It is what I am good at. When I find a place where the lines meet, I will tell you."

The guard coughs again.

"Go," says Wenyuan. He closes his hand, for an instant, round the boy's wrist, and lets go. "Eat. Sleep. Do not use anything you could do with your head."

"I have the talismans."

"Good." A faint, tired nod. "That was a joke, Jian. You may laugh."

He does not. But something in his chest loosens, a little, and he finds that he is smiling at the stone floor when he gets up.

* * *

He reads the letter on the steps of the Hall of Open Session, before he goes up the hill, with his back against a cold stone pillar and the packet open on his knee.

His mother's is a single page. It has no numbers, as promised. It has a description of the weather, which is clearing, and a note that Wenshi's Keepers have begun to drill without Hu's shouting, which is a sign of either progress or despair. It has a sentence about Pebble: Tell her the cat in the granary has had kittens. She will not like it. Tell her anyway. It ends: Eat something.

Lin Yue's is at the bottom, in a round, careful, child's hand, with every letter standing on its own.

How many were nice to you? Write a number.

He looks at it for a long time. Then he takes the stub of charcoal that every Outer disciple carries for the duty slate, and the back of the bamboo slip with the point on it, and writes, very small, under his sister's line:

Three. A boy with a rice cake. A keeper who did not say. Feng.

He folds it, and tucks it into the packet, and sits a moment longer in the shade of the pillar. It is not a large number. It is, he thinks, the first honest figure he has entered in this place.

* * *

The Pill Hall is the oldest building in the Outer Court, and it smells of burnt sugar.

It stands on a spur of rock halfway up the mountain, a great, low, tiled pavilion with a roof of dark green glass and a courtyard of nine furnaces, each the height of a house. Smoke rises from them in slow gray columns. Servants in leather aprons trot between them with baskets of roots and trays of pill-molds. A gong sounds, somewhere, deep in the building. A faint, hot, dry, sweet air flows out of the doors, like the breath of an animal.

He has come at noon, after the terrace, with the slip of bamboo in his sleeve and a speech he has rehearsed.

The steward at the door is a young man with a bandaged hand and an air of deep, harassed fatigue. He does not look up from his abacus.

"Registrations are closed."

"I am not here to register. I would like to apply as an apprentice."

"Apprentices are chosen by the Elders. At the new moon." The abacus clicks. "You are a first-year. An Outer. You have no craft. You have not been taught." He glances up, finally, and the glance is flat and incurious. "What is your name?"

"Lin Jian."

The abacus stops.

"The Mirror boy," says the steward. "The nine."

"Yes."

"I did not know they let nines apply." He considers this, with the weary air of a man whose job is to find the rule that applies. He pulls a thin wooden book from under the counter and thumbs it open. "Outer disciples may learn the Level 1 legacy. That is all. The Pill Hall teaches three recipes to any Outer who applies: Breath-Gathering, Marrow Wash, Blood Seal. They are the foundation. A disciple who masters them may, in time, be considered for the Level 2." He taps the page. "That requires an Elder's leave. And twenty points, for the fee."

"Twenty."

"Twenty. And an Elder who will say he wants you."

A patron, thinks Jian. And a price.

"Which Elders take apprentices?"

"At present? One." The steward lowers his voice. "Elder Bai. He is the master of the Hall. He has taken no apprentice in nine years. He does not like children. He does not like most adults." A very slight, painful smile. "He likes pills."

"How might I be seen?"

"You apply. You wait." The steward closes the book. "Or you are brought. That is how it is done, Disciple. An Elder who does not know a boy will not look at him, and an Elder who is introduced to a boy..." He lifts a shoulder. "It is the way the Sect works. The introduction is the thing."

"By whom?"

"Anyone with a name." He glances, meaningfully, toward the Outer Affairs Hall, whose red roof can be seen from the door, a hundred paces down the hill. "I would not like to say."

He goes back to his abacus.

Jian stands for a moment in the doorway of the Pill Hall, with the hot sweet air on his face. In the courtyard, a servant is pouring something into a mold, and the smell is rising, a thick, clean, stinging smell, like a clean sickroom in summer, and under it, so faint that he almost mistakes it for memory, the green bitter note of Ninefold marrow.

I do not have twenty points, he thinks. I have twenty-nine in debt. I have no Elder. I do not know a single person in the mountain with a name who is not a Deacon with a smile.

It is an exact description of a trap.

He walks back down the hill.

* * *

Mo Lian is waiting at the foot of the path, under a plum tree, with a flask of tea and two cups.

He has set them on a flat stone, in the shade, with a little folding stool for each of them, and he rises as the boy approaches, with a beaming, helpless delight, as a man greets a favorite nephew.

"Disciple Lin! What good fortune. I was just passing."

"Deacon."

"Sit, sit. You have had a long morning. I heard about the terrace. Overseer Han does not give out a point lightly." He pours. The tea is pale green, and steams. "And the Pill Hall! So soon. I am not surprised. A boy with your gifts. It is the proper ambition."

He has been watching, Jian thinks. He has watched every step. It does not surprise him.

"I have not been accepted," he says.

"No. How could you be?" The Deacon sighs. "It is a hard door. It is guarded by three things: a fee, a patron, and a name. You have none of them. I do not say that to wound you. I say it because I wish to help." He sips. "It is a great pity, when a boy of promise is turned away from a door he might have walked through."

"I am sure it is."

"And I think I might manage it."

He says it lightly. It is the most delicate offer Jian has ever heard. It is a thread, drawn so fine that it vanishes in the light.

"I am a Deacon of the Outer Affairs Hall," says Mo Lian. "I am not an Elder. I have not the rank to take a Personal disciple. But I am under the protection of a house, and that house is... considerable." A small, modest wave. "I could speak for you. I could see that the fee was paid, and the debt forgiven, and that a certain Elder, who is fond of me, was reminded that an exceptional boy was in want of a master. I could ask for a better courtyard. I could see that you were protected." The smile is wide and soft. "There are, you understand, a great many ways in which a boy may be unhappy, in a place like this. I would be glad to see that none of them befell you."

Protected, thinks Jian. From what? From a knot under a bed?

"That is very kind," he says.

"It is no more than my duty."

"And the Deacon would ask..."

"Oh, so little." The hands open, spread, empty. The thumbs, Jian notes, are inked to the knuckle. "It is not a price. It is a favor. A friendly thing, between two persons who understand each other." He leans a little closer. "You are of the Lin clan. Of Green Pine Hill. I am told it has a garden."

The tea has stopped steaming.

It is a very small thing. It might be the wind. But the cup in Jian's hand is suddenly colder than it was, and the shade under the plum tree is a little darker, and somewhere in the back of his head, a dry, dispassionate voice that belongs to a woman in a granary loft says, quite clearly: A Deacon's smile is a price. Ask what it costs.

"A garden," he says carefully. "Yes. A small one. It is held in trust by the Court."

"Quite so. Quite so. I would not dream of asking you to do anything improper." The Deacon's voice is warm and sweet as honey. "I only wonder, from time to time, whether a boy with so much in the way of access... might find it possible to bring a little something. A seedling. A root. A leaf, now and again, for a friend. Nothing that would be missed. Nothing that would trouble the Court."

A seedling, thinks Jian.

He sits perfectly still, with the cold cup in his hands.

The Garden's yield is down by a tenth. A Court deputy has written cause unknown in a margin. An inspector has promised, over a well, not to file. Wenyuan has lied to an officer of the Court, for a boy, in a voice he did not know he possessed. And a round, soft, smiling man with rust-colored ink under his thumbnails is asking, with the greatest delicacy, for the one thing in the whole of the Lin clan's world that the trust forbids.

He does not want Heartroot, he thinks. He wants the beds. He wants to know what is in them.

Who wants to know?

"Think it over," says Mo Lian gently. He rises, brushing a petal from his sleeve. "There is no hurry. The new moon is eleven days away. The fee is due at the new moon." He bows, a small, warm, courteous bow. "I look forward to your answer, Disciple Lin. I do so hope it is the one I expect."

He goes away up the hill, humming, with the flask in his hand.

Jian sits under the plum tree for a long time, with the tea going cold at his knee.

He has not drunk. He turns the cup in his fingers, and sees, on the rim, where the Deacon's thumb rested as he poured, a single smudge of rust-brown ink. He lifts it to his face. It does not smell of ink. It smells, very faintly, of iron.
